item.title: Tricky agreement: a number of, neither of, the majority
item.explanation_text: In careful writing, the verb agrees with the real head of the subject, not with the nearest noun: The quality of the photos is poor. Phrases such as along with, as well as and together with do not change the subject: The director, as well as her assistants, is attending. A number of + plural noun takes a plural verb (A number of problems have arisen), but the number of takes a singular verb (The number of applicants has doubled). Each, either and neither (of) take a singular verb in formal style: Neither of the reports mentions the cost. Words like majority, half, the rest and fractions agree with the noun after of: Half of the money was stolen; half of the students were absent. An amount seen as one unit takes a singular verb: Ten kilometres is a long way to walk. With either ... or and neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the manager nor the staff were informed.
item.contrast_text: Compare: The number of students in the group is small. A number of students in the group are from abroad.
item.common_error_pattern: Making the verb agree with the nearest noun instead of the real subject, e.g. 'The list of requirements are online.'
